seo_title: Sample Land Work | Annotated Ownership Report & Runsheet
meta_description: A fictional land file from first deed to signed lease and resolved heirship, with reader's notes explaining what each part of the report decides.
page_subtitle: One fictional tract, from the first deed to a signed lease and a resolved heirship.
intro:
Most land work ends in a few documents: a runsheet that lists every instrument in the chain, an ownership report that states who owns what and what stands in the way, and, once a lease is taken, an acquisition report that tells the client exactly what was bought. When the record leaves a question open, a supplemental report closes it.

The file below follows one fictional tract through all four, with reader's notes beside each document.
fiction_notice: Everything on this page is fictional. The county, township, people, companies, tract, dollar figures, and recording references were invented for illustration and do not describe any real property, owner, or transaction.
format_note: Formats vary by client and by state. We work in your templates or in ours. The content stays the same: every instrument accounted for, every open question stated as open.

mor.title: Mineral Ownership Report

fields.label: Description
fields.value: 62.40 acres, more or less, Whitmore Township, Alder County, Pennsylvania, Tax Parcel 14-006-021, being the same land conveyed by deed recorded in Record Book 1042, Page 677.

mineral_owners.name: Daniel W. Hallbeck
mineral_owners.status: Appears open. Last lease: Operator A, LLC, effective 05/01/2012, 5 year primary term, option to extend not exercised of record. Recorded RB 1388, Page 102. See Notes 3 and 4.

mineral_owners.name: Heirs of Marian H. Oster
mineral_owners.status: Unleased. Heirship not established. See Note 5.

surface_owners.name: Daniel W. Hallbeck
surface_owners.comments: Subject to open mortgage. See Note 4.

notes: Limited search. At the client's instruction the record was run forward from the 1921 deed into Jonas P. Hallbeck. Earlier title was not examined. Indexes searched: Recorder of Deeds, Register of Wills, and Prothonotary.

The 1921 deed excepts and reserves "all coal and other minerals." Oil and gas are not named. Whether that reservation reaches oil and gas is a legal question and is referred to the examining attorney. Ownership above is shown on the assumption that oil and gas passed to the grantee.

Two prior oil and gas leases appear of record (1968 and 2012). No well, unit declaration, production, or extension was found for either, and neither has been released. Both appear to have expired by their own terms. Recorded releases or an affidavit of non-production are recommended.
A 2016 mortgage from Daniel W. Hallbeck to Alder County Savings Bank is open of record. No satisfaction was found. Subordination should be considered at leasing.

Marian H. Oster took a one-quarter oil and gas interest under her father's 1961 estate. Nothing further appears in her name in Alder County. She is believed to have died in 2011 while living out of state. No estate, affidavit of heirship, or conveyance is of record. This interest cannot be leased until heirship is established.
The coal estate was severed in 1921 and was not examined.
mor.report_disclaimer: This report is a landman's summary of the public record. It is not an attorney's title opinion and carries no warranty of title.

annotations.text: Every report states what was searched and what was not. This one was run from 1921 forward at the client's request, and it says so. A report that does not state its limits cannot be relied on.
Ownership is carried as a decimal to six places because royalty is paid on it. 0.750000 of 62.40 acres is 46.80 net acres. The bonus check and every royalty payment follow that number.
"Appears open" means no lease of record is still holding the interest. It says "appears" because the record can only show what was filed.
The notes are the part of a report that gets read most closely. Each one is a question the record raises, and what it would take to close it.

annotations.text: A runsheet lists every instrument affecting the tract in the order it was recorded. Nothing is left out because it looks unrelated. The mortgage and the old leases are here because each one can change who has to sign and who gets paid.

This column is where ownership of the minerals separates from ownership of the surface. One sentence in a 1954 deed is the reason the person who owns this land today does not own all of the gas under it.
The last column carries ownership forward after every instrument, so anyone can check the arithmetic without repeating the search.

annotations.text: Nothing in this section came from the county deed index. It came from an out-of-state probate file, published obituaries, and sworn statements from family members. That is where most hard title questions get answered.
One quarter interest became four owners in three households. Each has to be found, each has to sign, and the decimals have to add back to 0.250000.
A finding is not finished until it says what has to be recorded to make it hold. This list is what turns research into title an operator can pay on.

simple_note: This file is short on purpose. One tract, eight instruments, one open question. That keeps the format easy to follow. Working files are longer, often much longer, and the method does not change. The last document shows what that method looks like when the record runs out.

how_to_read.title: If you own land or minerals
how_to_read.text: Read the notes beside each document. They say what each part decides: who has to sign, who gets paid, and on what share. This is the same report an operator would receive. Nothing has been simplified.

how_to_read.title: If you run a land department
how_to_read.text: Turn the notes off and read it as a deliverable. Check the limits stated in the header, how open items are carried, and whether the decimals tie from the runsheet to the ownership report to the lease report.

hard_files.headline: What Makes a File Hard
hard_files.intro: The sample has one open question. Most files have several. These are the ones we see most, and none of them is unusual for us.

items.title: Heirs who never opened an estate
items.text: An owner dies, the family keeps paying the taxes, and nothing is ever filed. The interest has to be traced through the family, across county and state lines, and put back on the record.

items.title: Minerals severed generations ago
items.text: A reservation in an old deed can leave the minerals with a family that has not owned the surface in a century. They do not appear in the current owner's chain, so they have to be found from the other direction.

items.title: Old leases that were never released
items.text: An expired lease with no release of record is still a question. The answer is in production records and unit filings, not in the deed books.

items.title: Interests that differ by depth or formation
items.text: One tract can have different owners, and different leases, at different depths. Each horizon has to be run as its own chain.

items.title: Tax sales, quiet title actions, and court records
items.text: Some of the chain sits in the prothonotary's office or the tax claim bureau and never reaches the deed index.

items.title: Royalty and overriding interests carved out along the way
items.text: A non-participating royalty or an override does not change who signs the lease, but it changes who gets paid, and it has to be carried through every later conveyance.
